claim: Food deprivation induces a linear current-voltage relationship of AMPAR-mediated excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in POMC neurons in mice.
source: Here, we show in mice that food deprivation induces a linear current-voltage relationship of AMPAR-mediated excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in POMC neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing I-V relationships in fasted vs fed mice.

claim: Inhibition of EPSCs by IEM-1460 diminished EPSC amplitude in the fed but not in the fasted state.
source: Inhibition of EPSCs by IEM-1460, an antagonist of calcium-permeable (Cp) AMPARs, diminished EPSC amplitude in the fed but not in the fasted state, suggesting entry of GluR2 subunits into the AMPA receptor complex during food deprivation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing differential effects of IEM-1460 on EPSC amplitude between fed and fasted states.

claim: GluR2 subunits enter the AMPA receptor complex during food deprivation.
source: Inhibition of EPSCs by IEM-1460, an antagonist of calcium-permeable (Cp) AMPARs, diminished EPSC amplitude in the fed but not in the fasted state, suggesting entry of GluR2 subunits into the AMPA receptor complex during food deprivation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects of IEM-1460 and represents an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Removal of extracellular calcium from ACSF decreased the amplitude of mEPSCs in the fed but not the fasted state.
source: Accordingly, removal of extracellular calcium from ACSF decreased the amplitude of mEPSCs in the fed but not the fasted state.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing mEPSC amplitudes in calcium-containing vs calcium-free ACSF.

claim: Ten days of high-fat diet exposure was accompanied by elevated leptin levels and increased POMC neuronal activity.
source: Ten days of high-fat diet exposure, which was accompanied by elevated leptin levels and increased POMC neuronal activity, resulted in increased expression of Cp-AMPARs on POMC neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations in the HFD paradigm.

claim: Ten days of high-fat diet exposure resulted in increased expression of Cp-AMPARs on POMC neurons.
source: Ten days of high-fat diet exposure, which was accompanied by elevated leptin levels and increased POMC neuronal activity, resulted in increased expression of Cp-AMPARs on POMC neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased rectification of AMPAR-EPSCs in HFD-fed mice.

claim: Entry of calcium via Cp-AMPARs is inherent to activation of POMC neurons.
source: Altogether, our results show that entry of calcium via Cp-AMPARs is inherent to activation of POMC neurons, which may underlie a vulnerability of these neurons to calcium overload while activated in a sustained manner during over-nutrition.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the collective experimental results presented in the study.

claim: POMC neurons may be vulnerable to calcium overload while activated in a sustained manner during over-nutrition.
source: Altogether, our results show that entry of calcium via Cp-AMPARs is inherent to activation of POMC neurons, which may underlie a vulnerability of these neurons to calcium overload while activated in a sustained manner during over-nutrition.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a potential consequence of the observed calcium entry via Cp-AMPARs.

claim: POMC-producing neurons in the arcuate nucleus (ARC) of the hypothalamus control satiety and glucose metabolism.
source: Proopiomelanocortin (POMC)-producing neurons in the arcuate nucleus (ARC) of the hypothalamus are well known to control satiety and glucose metabolism (Horvath, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The ablation of POMC neurons induces marked obesity in animals.
source: The ablation of POMC neurons or the depletion of the POMC gene induces marked obesity in animals (Gropp et al., 2005; Smart et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2005; Yaswen et al., 1999)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The depletion of the POMC gene induces marked obesity in animals.
source: The ablation of POMC neurons or the depletion of the POMC gene induces marked obesity in animals (Gropp et al., 2005; Smart et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2005; Yaswen et al., 1999)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Optical activation of POMC neurons through channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) selectively expressed in these neurons diminishes feeding behavior.
source: while the optical activation of POMC neurons through channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) selectively expressed in these neurons diminishes feeding behavior (Aponte et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: POMC neurons integrate peripheral metabolic signals such as leptin, insulin and glucose.
source: POMC neurons integrate peripheral metabolic signals such as leptin, insulin and glucose, and alter other circuits to adjust behavior and autonomic regulation, in part, through melanocortin receptor signaling (Cone, 2005; Gao and Horvath, 2007; Horvath, 2006; Koch et al., 2015; Mountjoy et al., 1992; Ollmann et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: POMC neurons alter other circuits to adjust behavior and autonomic regulation, in part, through melanocortin receptor signaling.
source: POMC neurons integrate peripheral metabolic signals such as leptin, insulin and glucose, and alter other circuits to adjust behavior and autonomic regulation, in part, through melanocortin receptor signaling (Cone, 2005; Gao and Horvath, 2007; Horvath, 2006; Koch et al., 2015; Mountjoy et al., 1992; Ollmann et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Synaptic transmission is required to regulate POMC neuronal activity and body weight.
source: In addition to peripheral metabolic signals, synaptic transmission is also required to regulate POMC neuronal activity and body weight (Branco et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Sensory detection of food inactivated Agouti-related protein (AgRP) neurons and activated POMC neurons in the ARC by fast neurotransmission.
source: Furthermore, recent studies showed that sensory detection of food inactivated Agouti-related protein (AgRP) neurons and activated POMC neurons in the ARC by fast neurotransmission (Betley et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The synaptic input organization on POMC neurons is plastic following the dynamic changes of the overall energy status of animals.
source: It was demonstrated that the synaptic input organization on POMC neurons is plastic following the dynamic changes of the overall energy status of animals (Horvath, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The number and transmission efficacy of glutamatergic synaptic inputs onto POMC neurons are increased by anorexigenic signals such as leptin and estrogen.
source: In this process, the number and transmission efficacy of glutamatergic synaptic inputs onto POMC neurons are increased by anorexigenic signals such as leptin and estrogen (Acuna-Goycolea and van den Pol, 2009; Gao et al., 2007; Horvath and Gao, 2005; Horvath et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2014; Pinto et al., 2004; Sotonyi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The frequency of mEPSCs was comparable in fasted and fed mice.
source: The frequency of mEPSCs was comparable in fasted and fed mice (fasting, 3.65 ± 0.61 Hz, n = 13; feeding, 4.08 ± 0.57 Hz, n = 14, p=0.61, unpaired t-test) (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The averaged median amplitude of mEPSCs tended to be smaller in fasted mice than in fed controls on normal chow.
source: The averaged median amplitude of mEPSCs tended to be smaller in fasted mice than in fed controls on normal chow (fasting, 13.46 ± 0.65 pA, n = 13; feeding, 16.37 ± 1.55 pA, n = 14, p=0.10, unpaired t-test) (Figure 1a,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, though the difference did not reach statistical significance.

claim: The distribution of mEPSC amplitude was significantly different between fasted and fed groups.
source: The distribution of amplitude was significantly different between fasted and fed groups (p<0.001, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Postsynaptic properties may be altered in POMC neurons in animals undergoing changes in their energy states.
source: These data indicate that postsynaptic properties may be altered in POMC neurons in animals undergoing changes in their energy states.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the mEPSC data presented.

claim: The AMPAR/NMDAR ratio showed no significant difference between POMC neurons of fasted and fed animals.
source: There was no significant difference between POMC neurons of fasted and fed animals (fasting, 1.672 ± 0.679, n = 6; feeding, 1.415 ± 0.136, n = 6, p=0.73, T-test) (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The eEPSC exhibited a significant increase in the rectification of the current-voltage (I-V) relationship of AMPARs in POMC neurons of fed mice compared to fasted animals.
source: However, the eEPSC recorded in the presence of NMDAR inhibitor, AP5 (50 µM) and GABAA receptor inhibitor, bicuculline (30 µM) exhibited a significant increase in the rectification of the current-voltage (I-V) relationship of AMPARs in POMC neurons of fed mice compared to fasted animals (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing I-V relationships.

claim: The RI of AMPAR-EPSC in POMC neurons was 0.59 ± 0.01 (n = 8) in fasted mice and 0.30 ± 0.03 (n = 7) in fed mice (p<0.05, unpaired t-test).
source: The RI of AMPAR-EPSC in POMC neurons was 0.59 ± 0.01 (n = 8) in fasted mice and 0.30 ± 0.03 (n = 7) in fed mice (p<0.05, unpaired t-test) (Figure 2c)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The rectification of AMPAR-EPSCs was more significant in fed mice than in fasted ones.
source: The RI of AMPAR-EPSC in POMC neurons was 0.59 ± 0.01 (n = 8) in fasted mice and 0.30 ± 0.03 (n = 7) in fed mice (p<0.05, unpaired t-test) (Figure 2c), indicating that the rectification of AMPAR-EPSCs was more significant in fed mice than in fasted ones.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the RI data.

claim: Fasting facilitates GluR2-containing AMPAR translocation to synapses on POMC neurons while feeding leads to an increased expression of GluR2-lacking AMPARs on POMC neurons.
source: This suggests that fasting facilitates GluR2-containing AMPAR translocation to synapses on POMC neurons while feeding leads to an increased expression of GluR2-lacking AMPARs on POMC neurons.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the rectification data.

claim: The AMPAR/NMDAR ratio was comparable in NPY/AgRP neurons between fasted and fed mice.
source: The AMPAR/NMDAR ratio (fasting, 3.427 ± 0.820, n = 6; feeding, 5.818 ± 1.891, n = 4, p=0.29, unpaired T-test) and RI of AMPAR-EPSCs (fasting, 0.281 ± 0.071, n = 8; feeding, 0.211 ± 0.051, n = 6, p=0.44, unpaired T-test) were comparable in NPY/AgRP neurons between fasted and fed mice (Figure 3)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The RI of AMPAR-EPSCs was comparable in NPY/AgRP neurons between fasted and fed mice.
source: The AMPAR/NMDAR ratio (fasting, 3.427 ± 0.820, n = 6; feeding, 5.818 ± 1.891, n = 4, p=0.29, unpaired T-test) and RI of AMPAR-EPSCs (fasting, 0.281 ± 0.071, n = 8; feeding, 0.211 ± 0.051, n = 6, p=0.44, unpaired T-test) were comparable in NPY/AgRP neurons between fasted and fed mice (Figure 3)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The change in the composition of AMPARs is selective to POMC neurons during different mouse feeding paradigms.
source: To test whether the change in the composition of AMPARs is selective to POMC neurons during the different mouse feeding paradigms, we examined the AMPAR/NMDAR ratio and rectification of AMPAR-EPSCs in neighboring NPY/AgRP neurons of fasted and fed mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison between POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons.

claim: The normalized eEPSC amplitudes were 84.3 ± 5.6% of baseline (n = 8) in fasted mice and 69.3 ± 5.3% of baseline (n = 7) in fed mice after IEM 1460 application.
source: The normalized eEPSC amplitudes were 84.3 ± 5.6% of baseline (n = 8) in fasted mice and 69.3 ± 5.3% of baseline (n = 7) in fed mice
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The inhibition of EPSC amplitude in POMC neurons induced by IEM 1460 was significantly greater in fed than fasted mice.
source: the inhibition of EPSC amplitude in POMC neurons induced by IEM 1460 was significantly greater in fed than fasted mice (p<0.05, unpaired one-tail T-test) (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: There are more GluR2-lacking AMPARs in POMC neurons in fed versus fasted mice.
source: This observation supports the premise that there are more GluR2-lacking AMPARs in POMC neurons in fed versus fasted mice.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the IEM 1460 experiment.

claim: The median and distribution of mEPSC amplitude was not significantly different between normal and Ca2+-free ACSF in POMC neurons of fasted mice.
source: In POMC neurons of fasted mice, the median and distribution of mEPSC amplitude was not significantly different between normal and Ca2+-free ACSF (normal ACSF, 13.46 ± 0.65 pA, n = 13; Ca2+-free ACSF, 11.64 ± 0.787, n = 9) (Figures 1a,c and 5a,b)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The averaged median and distribution of mEPSC amplitude was significantly decreased in Ca2+-free ACSF than in normal ACSF in POMC neurons from fed mice.
source: while the averaged median and distribution of mEPSC amplitude was significantly decreased in Ca2+ -free ACSF than in normal ACSF in POMC neurons from fed mice (normal ACSF, 16.37 ± 1.55 pA, n = 14; Ca2+-free ACSF, 10.93 ± 0.4866 pA, n = 9, p<0.05 unpaired t-test) (Figures 1a,c and 5a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Averaged median and distribution of mEPSC amplitudes without extracellular calcium were not significantly different between POMC neurons of fed and fasted groups.
source: Notably, averaged median and distribution of mEPSC amplitudes without extracellular calcium were not significantly different between POMC neurons of fed and fasted groups [p=0.456 for average mEPSC amplitude (unpaired T-test), p=0.70 for distribution (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test)] (Figure 5c,d)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Extracellular calcium ions contribute more to the amplitude of mEPSCs in POMC neurons of fed but not fasted mice.
source: indicating that extracellular calcium ions contribute more to the amplitude of mEPSCs in POMC neurons of fed but not fasted mice.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the calcium-free ACSF experiments.

claim: The calcium-free ACSF results are consistent with GluR2 entry into the synapses in the fasted state.
source: This is consistent with GluR2 entry into the synapses in the fasted state.
evidence: This claim is an inference connecting the experimental results to the hypothesis about GluR2 entry.

claim: In fed mice, β endorphin secretion significantly increased in hypothalamic slices treated with AMPA compared to aCSF, AMPA + IEM 1460 and IEM 1460.
source: In fed mice, β endorphin secretion significantly increased in hypothalamic slices treated with AMPA compared to aCSF, AMPA + the Cp-AMPA blocker IEM 1460 and IEM 1460 (Figure 6a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from beta-endorphin secretion assays.

claim: In fasted mice, β endorphin levels were comparable in hypothalamic slices treated with AMPA compared to aCSF, AMPA + IEM 1460 and IEM 1460.
source: In fasted mice, β endorphin levels were comparable in hypothalamic slices treated with AMPA compared to aCSF, AMPA + IEM 1460 and IEM 1460 (Figure 6b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from beta-endorphin secretion assays.

claim: β endorphin could be released via activation of Cp-AMPAR, which is dominant in POMC neurons under fed condition.
source: This suggests that β endorphin could be released via activation of Cp-AMPAR, which is dominant in POMC neurons under fed condition.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the beta-endorphin secretion experiments.

claim: The RI was 0.34 ± 0.04 (n = 8) in POMC neurons of the ARC of HFD fed mice and 0.46 ± 0.03 (n = 9) in ND fed mice.
source: The RI was 0.34 ± 0.04 (n = 8) in POMC neurons of the ARC of HFD fed mice and 0.46 ± 0.03 (n = 9) in ND fed mice. This represents a significant difference in RI (p<0.01, T-test, Figure 7c) between these two groups
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The rectification of AMPAR-EPSCs was significantly enhanced in HFD mice compared to ND mice.
source: This represents a significant difference in RI (p<0.01, T-test, Figure 7c) between these two groups, suggesting that the rectification of AMPAR-EPSCs was significantly enhanced in HFD mice.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the RI data from HFD vs ND mice.

claim: Cp-AMPAR expression at synaptic sites on POMC neurons is enhanced by HFD.
source: These data indicate that Cp-AMPAR expression at synaptic sites on POMC neurons is enhanced by HFD.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the HFD rectification data.

claim: The mEPSC amplitude decreased after removing extracellular calcium in POMC neurons in both HFD and ND conditions.
source: The mEPSC amplitude decreased after removing extracellular calcium in POMC neurons in both HFDs [Ca2+ present: 15.91 ± 2.17, Ca2+, absent: 12.39 ± 1.33 pA (mean ± SEM), p<0.05 for averaged median amplitude (paired T-test), p<0.001 for distribution (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test), n = 8, Figure 6d,e] and ND conditions [Ca2+ present: 16.06 ± 1.05, Ca2+ absent: 14.19 ± 1.27 pA (mean ± SEM), p<0.05 for averaged median amplitude (paired T-test), p<0.001 for distribution (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test), n = 8, Figure 7f,g].
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: mEPSC amplitude without Ca2+ was smaller in HFD mice compared to ND.
source: Interestingly, mEPSC amplitude without Ca2+ was smaller in HFD mice compared to ND [p<0.001 for distribution (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) Figure 6e]
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: mEPSC amplitude with Ca2+ did not show a significant difference between HFD and ND groups.
source: whereas those with Ca2+ did not show a significant difference between the two groups [p=0.56 for distribution (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) Figure 7f,g].
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Short-term HFD application induces higher calcium permeability through Cp-AMPAR expression on POMC neurons more than ND does.
source: These data suggest that short-term HFD application induces higher calcium permeability through Cp-AMPAR expression on POMC neurons more than ND does.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the HFD calcium-free ACSF experiments.

claim: The RI was 0.489 ± 0.062 (n = 8) in fasted plus saline-treated mice, but significantly less in the fasted plus leptin-treated mice: 0.296 ± 0.057 (n = 7).
source: The RI was 0.489 ± 0.062 (n = 8) in fasted plus saline-treated mice, but significantly less in the fasted plus leptin-treated mice: 0.296 ± 0.057 (n = 7). (Figure 8b,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The RI was 0.585 ± 0.050 (n = 3) without leptin treatment and 0.212 ± 0.063 (n = 3) with leptin treatment in slices from fasted mice.
source: The RI was 0.585 ± 0.050 (n = 3) without leptin treatment and 0.212 ± 0.063 (n = 3) with leptin treatment in slices from fasted mice, thus showing a significantly smaller RI in leptin-treated POMC neurons compared to the control and systemic leptin application (Figure 8d,e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro leptin treatment.

claim: Leptin treatment showed a significantly smaller RI in leptin-treated POMC neurons compared to the control and systemic leptin application.
source: The RI was 0.585 ± 0.050 (n = 3) without leptin treatment and 0.212 ± 0.063 (n = 3) with leptin treatment in slices from fasted mice, thus showing a significantly smaller RI in leptin-treated POMC neurons compared to the control and systemic leptin application (Figure 8d,e).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the in vitro leptin treatment data.

claim: Rapamycin treatment caused a significant increase in the RI in POMC neurons compared to saline injected fed mice.
source: Rapamycin treatment caused a significant increase in the RI in POMC neurons compared to saline injected fed mice [rapamycin group: 0.817 ± 0.104 (n = 7), saline group: 0.403 ± 0.066 (n = 7)] (Figure 9a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The ARC slices from fasted mice incubated with 100 µM leucine for 4 hr showed a significant decrease in RI.
source: Furthermore, the ARC slices from fasted mice incubated with 100 µM leucine (an activator of mTOR) for 4 hr showed a significant decrease in RI [leucine group: 0.301 ± 0.033 (n = 6), control group: 0.498 ± 0.449 (n = 6), p<0.01, T-test)] (Figure 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The leptin-mTOR pathway contributes to the enhanced expression of Cp-AMPARs in POMC neurons in the state of positive energy balance.
source: These results provide evidence that the leptin-mTOR pathway contributes to the enhanced expression of Cp-AMPARs in POMC neurons in the state of positive energy balance (fed animals).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the rapamycin and leucine experiments.

claim: The RI on the fed group did not show a significant difference between the control at 10 or 15 min after rupture of the membrane with PD98095 treatment.
source: The RI on the fed group did not show a significant difference between the control at 10 or 15 min after rupture of the membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ERK inhibitor experiments.

claim: The RI on the fasted group decreased significantly at 10 min after rupture with PD98095 treatment.
source: By comparison, the RI on the fasted group decreased significantly at 10 min after rupture [fasted group: 0.60 ± 0.098 at 1 min, 0.353 ± 0.038 at 10 min, 0.344 ± 0.048 at 15 min, (n = 7) p<0.01 in 1 min vs. 10 min and 1 min vs. 15 min (two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and Tukey multiple comparison posthoc test), fed group: 0.426 ± 0.064 at 1 min, 0.409 ± 0.068 at 10 min, 0.332 ± 0.051 at 15 min (n = 7)] (Figure 11a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: ERK phosphorylation promotes GluR2-containing Ci-AMPAR translocation to the synaptic membrane.
source: These data suggest that ERK phosphorylation promotes GluR2-containing Ci-AMPAR translocation to the synaptic membrane.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the ERK inhibitor experiments.

claim: mEPSC amplitude which reflects efficiency of the synaptic transmission at the postsynaptic site is higher in POMC neurons in the ARC in fed animals than in fasted animals.
source: In this study, we showed that mEPSC amplitude which reflects efficiency of the synaptic transmission at the postsynaptic site is higher in POMC neurons in the ARC in fed animals than in fasted animals
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the mEPSC data.

claim: Under a normal feeding paradigm a higher efficiency of glutamatergic transmission onto POMC neurons may lead to the activation of POMC neurons.
source: suggesting that under a normal feeding paradigm a higher efficiency of glutamatergic transmission onto POMC neurons may lead to the activation of POMC neurons.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a potential consequence of the observed higher mEPSC amplitude.

claim: More GluR2-lacking, Ca2+-permeable AMPARs are expressed on the surface of POMC neurons in animals under normal feeding and HFD.
source: Therefore, our results demonstrate that more GluR2-lacking, Ca2+-permeable AMPARs are expressed on the surface of POMC neurons in animals under normal feeding and HFD.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: GluR1 but not GluR2 is expressed in ARC neurons under a normal feeding paradigm.
source: This is consistent with a previous study showing that GluR1 but not GluR2 is expressed in ARC neurons under a normal feeding paradigm (Bowie and Mayer, 1995; Gao et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GluR2 is not expressed in certain types of neurons in many brain areas under basal conditions.
source: There is ample evidence that GluR2 is not expressed in certain types of neurons in many brain areas, including neocortical, hippocampal, and amygdaloidal fast-spiking interneurons, cerebellar stellate cells, dorsal horn interneurons, large striatal cholinergic neurons, bushy and stellate cells of the cochlear nucleus, spinothalamic projection neurons, and retinal amacrine cells, in addition to Bergmann glia and oligodendrocyte precursor cells of the cerebellum under basal conditions.
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about GluR2 expression patterns.

claim: Dendrites of POMC neurons were aspiny.
source: Studies showed that dendrites of POMC neurons were aspiny (Hentges et al., 2005; Isaac et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cerebellar stellate cells express Cp-AMPAR-dependent and NMDAR-independent LTD after high-frequency stimulation.
source: For example, cerebellar stellate cells express Cp-AMPAR-dependent and NMDAR-independent LTD after high-frequency stimulation, which includes the replacement of Cp-AMPARs by Ca2+-impermeable GluR2-containing AMPARs after the expression of LTD (Liu and Cull-Candy, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The depletion of NMDARs specifically in POMC neurons did not have a significant effect on feeding and energy expenditure in animals.
source: It is important to note that in a recent study, the depletion of NMDARs specifically in POMC neurons did not have a significant effect on feeding and energy expenditure in animals, suggesting that NMDARs may not be required for the functions exerted by POMC neurons (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: NMDARs may not be required for the functions exerted by POMC neurons.
source: It is important to note that in a recent study, the depletion of NMDARs specifically in POMC neurons did not have a significant effect on feeding and energy expenditure in animals, suggesting that NMDARs may not be required for the functions exerted by POMC neurons (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the cited study on NMDAR depletion.

claim: HFD did not induce weight change until at least 2 weeks after starting it.
source: Under these conditions, it is expected that the secondary effects originating from obesity by HFD application were minimized, because HFD did not induce weight change until at least 2 weeks after starting it (Lin et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Circulating levels of leptin have been reported to increase at 3 days after HFD application.
source: Circulating levels of leptin have been reported to increase at 3 days after HFD application (Wang et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: POMC neurons were rewired in a polysialic acid molecule-dependent fashion during HFD, and showed increasing frequency of EPSCs but no change in amplitude of PSCs.
source: In this period, POMC neurons were rewired in a polysialic acid molecule-dependent fashion, and showed increasing frequency of EPSCs but no change in amplitude of PSCs (Benani et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The levels of circulating leptin decline under fasting conditions.
source: Under fasting conditions, the levels of circulating leptin decline, leading to a reduction in the number and efficacy of excitatory inputs onto POMC neurons (Ahima et al., 1996; Pinto et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Fasting leads to a reduction in the number and efficacy of excitatory inputs onto POMC neurons.
source: Under fasting conditions, the levels of circulating leptin decline, leading to a reduction in the number and efficacy of excitatory inputs onto POMC neurons (Ahima et al., 1996; Pinto et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Leptin promotes the expression of GluR2-lacking Ca2+-permeable AMPARs at the postsynaptic site.
source: Thus, leptin promotes the expression of GluR2-lacking Ca2+-permeable AMPARs at the postsynaptic site.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the leptin treatment experiments.

claim: mTOR was shown to be downstream of the leptin signal via PI3K pathway, in order to suppress food intake and regulate POMC expression in the hypothalamus.
source: mTOR was shown to be downstream of the leptin signal via PI3K pathway, in order to suppress food intake and regulate POMC expression in the hypothalamus (Blouet et al., 2009; Cota et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Leptin directly regulates Cp-AMPAR translocation by increasing GluR1 expression at synapses of hippocampal CA1 neurons via PTEN inhibition and activation of the PI3K pathway.
source: There is also evidence that leptin directly regulates Cp-AMPAR translocation by increasing GluR1 expression at synapses of hippocampal CA1 neurons via PTEN inhibition and activation of the PI3K pathway (Moult et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Leptin removed Cp-AMPARs after LTP induction via calcium/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase and calcinurin at certain time points after induction of LTP.
source: Leptin also removed Cp-AMPARs after LTP induction via calcium/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase and calcinurin at certain time points after induction of LTP (Moult et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: mTOR-mediated protein translation is needed to establish several types of long-lasting synaptic changes and long-term memory.
source: Additionally, growing evidence has shown that mTOR-mediated protein translation is needed to establish several types of long-lasting synaptic changes and long-term memory (see review [Costa-Mattioli et al., 2009]).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) induced GluR1 translation that required mTOR activation in hippocampal CA1 neurons.
source: For example, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which is essential for LTP, induced GluR1 translation that required mTOR activation in hippocampal CA1 neurons (Fortin et al., 2012; Slipczuk et al., 2009).

claim: mTOR-mediated autophagy controls the GluR1 subunit.
